summary: Brass: Birmingham is a dense economic Euro where you build canal and rail networks while flipping industry tiles for points across two historical eras. It's a tight, punishing engine of loans, markets, and network-building that rewards careful sequencing.
praised: Extremely high replayability and strategic depth
Gorgeous, thematic production and map design
criticised: Steep learning curve, unforgiving for new players
Can feel like multiplayer solitaire with only indirect interaction

interaction.kind: fighting over shared coal/iron markets and contested network links/city spots
interaction.detail: Coal and iron are drawn from shared, depleting markets that everyone's builds affect, and canal/rail links plus city spaces are limited, so a good move is very often chosen specifically to deny an opponent the resource or link they were counting on. The board and markets are almost entirely shared state rather than private tableaus.
interaction.said: widely described as "brutal," "cutthroat," and "vicious" — players frequently note you can get "screwed" by others exhausting the resource markets or blocking your network

subsystems: industry development (building and flipping industry tiles)
sources: flipped industry tile VP, canal era
flipped industry tile VP, rail era
scoring.how_you_win: The canal era ends when its card deck is exhausted and links/flipped industries are scored, then the rail era plays out the same way and is scored again; add leftover money converted to VP, and the highest total wins.

theme.said: 'Brass is a spreadsheet with a top hat,' 'the goods could be cubes of any color,' though some defend the canal-to-rail era shift and the beer requirement as historically grounded
theme.why: the beer-as-required-resource-to-sell-goods mechanic and the hard pivot from canal-era to rail-era networks nod at real infrastructure history, but the core loop of link-building, demand flags, and card-driven actions is an interchangeable network/majority puzzle

style.why: A pure economic engine of loans, industries and route-building with symmetric player options, negligible randomness, and victory by points at a fixed game-end trigger
